A complete guide to using the scan feature to detect diseases in your cattle.

How to Scan

Open SapiSehat and make sure you are on the Scan tab. Point the camera at the cattle you want to examine.

Tips for Taking Good Photos

• Take the photo from 1–2 meters away so the entire body is clearly visible
• Ensure adequate lighting and avoid shadows on the body
• Position the camera parallel to the cattle's body, not from above
• Avoid blurry, too distant, or obstructed images
• Focus on areas showing symptoms (mouth, hooves, or skin)

After Taking a Photo

The app will process the image and display the early detection result within seconds. Results include the early indication of detected disease, confidence score, and initial treatment recommendations.

You can also select an image from your gallery by tapping the gallery icon at the bottom of the camera screen.
Differences between online and offline inference modes, and when to use each.

Online Mode

In online mode, the image is sent to the server for analysis using the full MobileNetV2 model. This mode requires a stable internet connection.

Online mode advantages:
• Higher accuracy using the full server-side model
• Automatic model updates without needing to update the app

Offline Mode

In offline mode, analysis is performed directly on your device using TensorFlow Lite. This mode works without an internet connection.

Offline mode advantages:
• Works in locations without internet signal
• Faster processing since no data is sent to the server
• Image data stays on your device (more private)

When to Use Each?

Use online mode when you have a stable internet connection and need the highest accuracy results. Use offline mode when in the field without signal or when you need instant results.

The app will automatically switch to offline mode if the server cannot be reached.
How to read confidence scores and understand the reliability of detection results.

Confidence Score

Every early detection result includes a confidence score as a percentage. This score indicates how certain the model is about the detection result.

Confidence Levels

• High (≥80%): The model is very confident in the result. Results can be relied upon for initial action.
• Medium (60–79%): The model is fairly confident, but it is recommended to rescan with a clearer photo or from a different angle.
• Low (<60%): The model is uncertain. Rescan with better photo conditions. If results remain low, consult a veterinarian immediately.

Per-Class Scores

Besides the main result, the app displays scores for each class (Healthy, FMD, LSD). This helps you see the distribution of possible indications.

When to Rescan?

• Confidence score below 60%
• Photo taken was blurry or poorly lit
• Result does not match visually observed symptoms

Important: Results from this app are an early detection aid, not a replacement for professional veterinary diagnosis.
Basic information about Foot and Mouth Disease, its causes, and impact on livestock.

What Is FMD?

Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD), known as PMK (Penyakit Mulut dan Kuku) in Indonesia, is a highly contagious acute viral disease caused by a virus from the genus Aphthovirus, family Picornaviridae. It affects all cloven-hoofed animals including cattle, buffalo, sheep, goats, and pigs.

Economic Impact

FMD causes enormous economic losses due to:
• Permanent weight loss in livestock
• Milk production decrease of 50–80%
• Reduced fertility and reproductive disorders
• High mortality in young animals
• Barriers to national and international livestock trade

Virus Characteristics

• Incubation period: 2–14 days
• Morbidity: can reach 100% in susceptible populations
• Mortality: generally low in adult animals (<5%), but high in calves (up to 50%)
• Virus can survive in the environment, bones, and dairy products

Source: Indonesian Ministry of Agriculture, WOAH (World Organisation for Animal Health)
Clinical signs of FMD in cattle from early to advanced stages.

Early Stage (Days 1–3)

• High fever (40–41°C)
• Drastically reduced appetite
• Sudden drop in milk production
• Cattle appear lethargic and reluctant to move

Vesicle Formation Stage (Days 3–7)

• Fluid-filled blisters/vesicles appear on:
 - Tongue, gums, and palate
 - Lips and nostrils
 - Skin between and above the hooves
 - Teats
• Excessive salivation (hypersalivation) with foaming
• Characteristic chewing sounds
• Lameness due to hoof lesions

Erosion Stage (Days 7–14)

• Vesicles rupture forming open erosions/wounds
• Oral lesions cause difficulty eating
• Hoof lesions cause severe lameness
• Risk of secondary bacterial infection

Signs in Calves

• Sudden death without blister symptoms (myocarditis)
• Higher mortality rate compared to adult cattle

Source: Indonesian Agricultural Extension, Agropustaka APVI
How FMD virus spreads and biosecurity measures to prevent outbreaks.

Transmission Routes

FMD virus spreads through:
• Direct contact with infected animals
• Air (aerosol) — virus can spread up to 60 km by wind
• Contaminated farm equipment
• Livestock transport vehicles
• Animal products (meat, milk, hides)
• Humans (clothing, footwear) who contacted sick animals

The virus enters through the mouth or nose, multiplies in the nasopharynx, then spreads through the bloodstream throughout the body.

Prevention Measures

1. Vaccination
• Conduct routine vaccination per government program
• Revaccinate every 6 months
• Ensure all livestock in the population are vaccinated

2. Farm Biosecurity
• Restrict access of people and vehicles to farm areas
• Provide disinfectant footbaths at farm entrances
• Use dedicated clothing and footwear for the farm
• Clean and disinfect equipment regularly

3. Quarantine
• Quarantine new livestock for at least 14 days
• Monitor for clinical signs during quarantine
• Do not mix new livestock with existing population until quarantine is complete

4. Movement Control
• Avoid purchasing livestock from outbreak areas
• Check animal health certificates when buying livestock
• Report suspicious livestock at markets to veterinary services

Source: Medion, Indonesian Ministry of Agriculture
Immediate steps to take when cattle show FMD symptoms.

Immediate Steps

1. Isolate
• Immediately separate cattle showing symptoms from healthy livestock
• Place in a separate quarantine pen
• Use separate equipment for sick animals

2. Report
• Immediately report to local livestock and animal health services
• Contact the nearest veterinarian
• Record the number of cattle showing symptoms

3. Wound Care
• Clean oral lesions with mild antiseptic solution
• Apply wound medication to hoof lesions
• Provide soft feed that is easy to eat (fine grass, wet concentrate)

4. Supportive Therapy
• Provide multivitamins and minerals to maintain immunity
• Ensure adequate clean drinking water
• Administer antibiotics if secondary infection occurs (by veterinary prescription)

Farm Disinfection

• Clean pens of manure and feed residue
• Spray with disinfectant (4% sodium carbonate or 0.2% citric acid)
• Disinfect equipment, vehicles, and footwear
• Repeat disinfection daily during outbreak

When to Call a Veterinarian?

• Immediately when first symptoms appear
• If there is sudden death in calves
• If lesions do not improve after 7 days of care
• If cattle refuse to eat for more than 3 days

Source: Medion, Kendal District Agricultural Service
Basic information about Lumpy Skin Disease, its causes, and spread in Indonesia.

What Is LSD?

Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD) is a viral disease affecting cattle and buffalo, caused by the Lumpy Skin Disease Virus (LSDV) from the family Poxviridae, genus Capripoxvirus.

Spread in Indonesia

LSD is an exotic disease originally endemic to Africa. Since 2012, it has spread to the Middle East, Southeast Europe, and Asia. In Indonesia, LSD cases have been reported and are a serious concern for farmers.

Impact on Livestock

• Significant decrease in milk production
• Reproductive disorders (infertility) in both male and female cattle
• Permanent skin damage reducing market value
• Weight loss
• Death from secondary infections (5–10% in severe cases)

Virus Characteristics

• Incubation period: 4–28 days
• Morbidity: 5–45% depending on population and vectors
• Virus can survive in skin scabs for up to 35 days
• All ages and breeds are susceptible, especially Bos taurus (Friesian, Jersey)

Source: Indonesian Agricultural Repository, WOAH, BBPKH Cinagara
Clinical signs of LSD in cattle, from early symptoms to complications.

Early Symptoms

• High fever (40–41°C) lasting several days
• Swollen lymph nodes (especially in neck and thigh)
• Watery eyes and nose
• Decreased appetite
• Sudden drop in milk production

Main Symptom — Skin Nodules

• Hard nodules appear on the skin, 2–5 cm in diameter
• Nodules spread across the body: head, neck, back, legs, udder, and scrotum
• Nodules are round, firm, and involve all skin layers
• Number varies from a few to hundreds
• Nodules may develop into open wounds (ulcers)

Complications

• Secondary bacterial infection of open wounds
• Leg swelling (edema)
• Pneumonia
• Reproductive disorders: abortion, temporary or permanent infertility
• Mastitis in dairy cattle

Differences from Other Skin Conditions

• LSD nodules involve all skin layers (not just the surface)
• Nodules are evenly distributed across the body
• Accompanied by fever and swollen lymph nodes
• Different from ordinary insect bites which are only superficial

Source: BBPKH Cinagara, Bogor District Livestock Service
How LSD spreads through insect vectors and effective prevention measures.

Transmission Routes

Primary LSD transmission is through blood-sucking insect vectors:
• Mosquitoes (Aedes, Culex)
• Blood-sucking flies (Stomoxys, Tabanus)
• Ticks (Rhipicephalus, Amblyomma)

Other transmission:
• Direct contact with skin lesions of infected animals
• Excretion through saliva, nasal discharge, blood, semen, and milk
• Contaminated equipment (needles, cutting tools)
• Contaminated feed and water

Prevention

1. Vector Control
• Install fly traps around the farm
• Use insecticides safe for livestock
• Remove standing water around the farm (mosquito breeding sites)
• Use nets or curtains on pens if possible
• Spray pens with insecticide regularly

2. Vaccination
• Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent LSD
• Use homologous (LSDV) or heterologous (Sheeppox/Goatpox) vaccines
• Vaccinate the entire cattle population in at-risk areas

3. Biosecurity
• Quarantine new livestock for at least 28 days
• Avoid sharing needles between animals
• Separate sick from healthy livestock
• Restrict livestock movement from infected areas

Source: Indonesian Agricultural Repository, BPPSDMP Library
Actions to take when cattle show LSD symptoms.

Immediate Steps

1. Isolate
• Immediately separate cattle showing skin nodules from healthy livestock
• Place in a separate pen protected from insects
• Use separate equipment (buckets, brushes, ropes)

2. Report
• Report to local livestock and animal health services
• Contact a veterinarian for examination and diagnosis confirmation
• Record the number of affected cattle and date of onset

3. Skin Lesion Care
• Clean ruptured nodules with antiseptic solution (povidone iodine)
• Apply antibiotic ointment to prevent secondary infection
• Keep the pen clean to prevent wound infection
• Protect wounds from flies with repellent

4. Supportive Therapy
• Provide anti-inflammatory medication to reduce fever and pain (by veterinary prescription)
• Administer systemic antibiotics if secondary infection occurs
• Ensure adequate nutrition with quality feed
• Provide additional vitamins and minerals

5. Vector Control in Isolation Pen
• Spray isolation pen with insecticide
• Install fly traps
• Clean manure regularly

When to Call a Veterinarian?

• Immediately when first skin nodules appear
• If cattle experience breathing difficulty
• If severe leg swelling occurs
• If pregnant cattle show signs of abortion
• If nodules spread rapidly to many animals

Source: Bogor District Livestock Service, Indonesian Agricultural Repository
Visual signs of healthy cattle as a baseline for early disease detection.

General Appearance

• Proportional body with good body condition (not too thin or fat)
• Shiny, clean, and even coat
• Elastic, clean skin without lesions, lumps, or scabs
• Bright, clear, and responsive eyes
• Moist nose without excessive discharge

Behavior

• Active and responsive to environment
• Good appetite and regular rumination
• Stands upright with all four feet flat
• Moves normally without lameness
• Normal interaction with other livestock

Normal Vital Signs

• Body temperature: 38–39.5°C
• Respiratory rate: 15–30 breaths per minute
• Heart rate: 40–80 beats per minute
• Rumination: 40–70 chews per minute

Production

• Stable milk production according to lactation period
• Weight gain meeting targets
• Regular reproductive cycle

When to Be Alert?

Check immediately if you notice:
• Sudden loss of appetite
• Fever (temperature above 39.5°C)
• Skin changes (lumps, lesions, hair loss)
• Lameness or reluctance to stand
• Excessive salivation
• Sudden drop in milk production

Daily routines and biosecurity measures to maintain livestock health.

Pen Management

• Clean pens of manure at least twice daily
• Ensure good pen ventilation for air circulation
• Provide clean feeding and drinking facilities
• Avoid overcrowding in pens
• Ensure pen floors are non-slip and easy to clean

Nutrition

• Provide quality forage (fresh grass, legumes)
• Add concentrate according to production needs
• Provide mineral blocks or mineral mix
• Ensure clean drinking water is available at all times
• Adjust feed portions to condition (pregnant, lactating, growing)

Vaccination Program

• Follow vaccination programs from local livestock services
• FMD vaccine: every 6 months
• LSD vaccine: per regional recommendations
• Anthrax, SE, Brucellosis vaccines: per schedule
• Record all vaccinations in livestock health cards

Vector Control

• Remove standing water around the farm
• Install fly traps
• Use safe insecticides regularly
• Cut wild grass around the farm
• Manage farm waste properly

Daily Biosecurity

• Restrict visitor access to farm areas
• Provide dedicated footwear and disinfectant footbaths
• Wash hands before and after handling livestock
• Use separate equipment for sick animals
• Quarantine new livestock for at least 14 days

Routine Checks

• Check livestock condition every morning and evening
• Measure body temperature if livestock appears lethargic
• Use SapiSehat for regular scans
• Schedule veterinary checkups at least twice yearly
• Record all health events in a recording book

Source: Indonesian Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock Services
